title: OPPOSITION: ATHLETIC CLUB PALERMO (003206555)
text:
OPPOSITION Nо B 3 206 555

Heineken España, S.A., Avenida de Andalucía, 1, 41007 Sevilla, Spain (opponent), represented by Fernández-Palacios Abogados, S.L.P.U., Plaza de la Magdalena, 9 - 4º, 41001 Sevilla, Spain (professional representative) 

a g a i n s t

Walter Bertucci, Via Marettimo, 5, 90040 Capaci (PA), Italy; Gaetano Conte, Via Serradifalco, 127, 90145 Palermo, Italy; Michele Lo Valvo, Via Bonanno Pietro, 13, 90142 Palermo, Italy; Davide La Fiora, S. Lorenzo, 149, 90146 Palermo, Italy; Salvatore Prestigiacomo, Via D'Antoni Andrea, 5, 90145 Palermo, Italy (applicants), all represented by Safety Brand S.R.L. Società tra Avvocati, Via Santo Stefano 58, Bologna, Italy (professional representative).

On 30/07/2026, the Opposition Division takes the following

DECISION:

REASONS

On 07/11/2023, the opponent filed an opposition against some of the goods and services of European Union trade mark application No 18 930 971  (figurative mark), namely against all the goods and services in Classes 32 and 41. The opposition is based on Spanish trade mark registrations No 4 023 520  (figurative mark) and No 4 055 374 'EL AGUILA' (word mark). The opponent invoked Articles 8(1)(b) and 8(5) EUTMR.

LIKELIHOOD OF CONFUSION — ARTICLE 8(1)(b) EUTMR

Pursuant to Article 8(1)(b) EUTMR, a likelihood of confusion exists if there is a risk that the public might believe that the goods or services in question, under the assumption that they bear the marks in question, come from the same undertaking or, as the case may be, from economically linked undertakings. Whether a likelihood of confusion exists depends on the appreciation in a global assessment of several factors, which are interdependent. These factors include the similarity of the signs, the similarity of the goods and services, the distinctiveness of the earlier mark, the distinctive and dominant elements of the conflicting signs, and the relevant public.

The opposition is based on more than one earlier trade mark. The Opposition Division finds it appropriate to first examine the opposition in relation to the opponent’s Spanish trade mark registration No 4 023 520  (figurative mark).

a) The goods and services

The goods on which the opposition is based are the following:

Class 32: Beers.

Following a limitation accepted by the Office on 04/07/2024, the contested goods and services are the following:

Class 32: Mineral and aerated waters; soft drinks; fruit juice beverages; syrups and other non-alcoholic preparations for making beverages; energy drinks.

Class 41: Fan club services; football academy services; organisation of sports events in the

field of football; health club services [health and fitness training]; training of sports players; health and wellness training; sports training; sporting services; entertainment services; sporting activities; organisation of sporting events; provision of information relating to sports; rental of sports grounds; organization of sports competitions; teaching; cultural activities; publication of printed matter and printed publications; providing online electronic publications, not downloadable; writing services for blogs.

The relevant factors relating to the comparison of the goods or services include, inter alia, their nature, their intended purpose, their method of use and whether they are in competition with each other or are complementary (‘the Canon criteria’). It is also necessary to take into account, besides the Canon criteria, other factors, namely distribution channels, the relevant public and the usual origin of the goods or services (02/06/2021, T‑177/20, Hispano Suiza / Hispano Suiza, EU:T:2021:312, § 21-22).

Contested goods in Class 32

The contested mineral and aerated waters; soft drinks; fruit juice beverages; and energy drinks are similar to the opponent's beers because they share the same purpose (i.e. to quench thirst) and are in competition with each other. Furthermore, they coincide in distribution channels and end users.

The contested syrups and other non-alcoholic preparations for making beverages all include ingredients for making home-made beer. These products are similar to the opponent’s beers, as they can be distributed in the same shops specialising in the retailing of beverage-related products, may target the same end users - in particular beer enthusiasts with an interest in homebrewing - and are normally manufactured by the same companies.

Contested services in Class 41

The contested fan club services; football academy services; organisation of sports events in the field of football; health club services [health and fitness training]; training of sports players; health and wellness training; sports training; sporting services; entertainment services; sporting activities; organisation of sporting events; provision of information relating to sports; rental of sports grounds; organization of sports competitions; teaching; cultural activities; publication of printed matter and printed publications; providing online electronic publications, not downloadable; writing services for blogs and the opponent's goods do not have the same natures, purposes or methods of use and they do not target the same relevant public or share the same distribution channels. Furthermore, the goods and services under comparison are not complementary to each other or in competition and they are not usually produced or provided by the same undertakings. Therefore, they are dissimilar.

b) Relevant public — degree of attention

The average consumer of the category of products concerned is deemed to be reasonably well informed and reasonably observant and circumspect. It should also be borne in mind that the average consumer’s degree of attention is likely to vary according to the category of goods or services in question (22/06/1999, C-342/97, Lloyd Schuhfabrik, EU:C:1999:323, § 26).

In the present case, the goods found to be similar target the general public. The degree of attention is considered to be average.

c) The signs

The relevant territory is Spain.

The global appreciation of the visual, aural or conceptual similarity of the marks in question must be based on the overall impression given by the marks, bearing in mind, in particular, their distinctive and dominant components (11/11/1997, C‑251/95, Sabèl, EU:C:1997:528, § 23).

The earlier mark consists of the following elements and aspects.

	The verbal element ‘EL ÁGUILA’, which means ‘the eagle’ in Spanish (). This meaning has no relationship with the relevant goods and, therefore, is distinctive to a normal degree.

	The typeface used to depict this element does not divert the attention of the consumer from the letters that it embellishes. Therefore, it is weak at best.

	Devices such as the earlier mark’s rectangular box are commonly used in the market to highlight the information contained in them and are not perceived as indications of commercial origin. Therefore, this element is non-distinctive.

	The figurative device above the mark’s verbal element will be perceived as a heavily-stylised depiction of an eagle’s head. This element is distinctive as it has no relationiship with the relevant goods.

	The earlier mark has no element that could be considered clearly more dominant than other elements. However, when signs consist of both verbal and figurative components, in principle, the verbal component of the sign usually has a stronger impact on the consumer than the figurative component. This is because the public does not tend to analyse signs and will more easily refer to the signs in question by their verbal element than by describing their figurative elements (14/07/2005, T‑312/03, SELENIUM-ACE / SELENIUM SPEZIAL A-C-E (fig.), EU:T:2005:289, § 37).

In its turn, the contested sign consists of the following elements and aspects.

	Regarding, the verbal elements ‘ATHLETIC CLUB PALERMO’: 

i) ‘ATHLETIC’ corresponds to a fairly basic English word, equivalent to the Spanish term atlético and, therefore, will be understood in this meaning; 

ii) The word ‘CLUB’ exists as such in Spanish and, therefore, will be understood in the meaning of ‘an organization founded by a group of people with shared interests and dedicated to various types of activities, primarily recreational, sports-related, or cultural’ (); 

iii) Part of the Spanish public will perceive ‘PALERMO’ as a reference to an Italian city, whereas another part as a coined word devoid of a specific meaning.

Considering the foregoing, the relevant public will perceive the above verbal elements as designating either a sports club named after the city of Palermo or a sports club simply bearing the fanciful name ‘Palermo’. In either case, these conceptual units bear no relationship whatsoever to the contested goods and are therefore distinctive to a normal degree.

	The contested sign’s double border. The outer border consists of a black circle, a basic geometric shape entirely devoid of any distinctive character. Inside it appears a pink semicircle that gradually widens towards its lower-left section. Although this figure is more complex than a simple circle and is not particularly common on the market, it nevertheless serves a purely decorative function and, accordingly, possesses only a low degree of distinctiveness.

	The figurative device above the mark’s verbal element will be perceived as a stylised depiction of an eagle’s head. This element is distinctive as it has no relationship with the relevant goods.

	The figurative element depicting an eagle must be regarded as the dominant element of the contested sign, by virtue of its position within the sign and its size relative to the other elements. However, as already explained, where signs consist of both word and figurative elements, the verbal element will generally have a stronger impact on consumers than the figurative element. Accordingly - and contrary to the opponent’s assertions - the impact of the verbal elements ‘ATHLETIC CLUB PALERMO’ cannot be underestimated, given that consumers will refer to the contested sign by means of those verbal elements.

Visually, the only point of contact between the signs is that they both include a stylised depiction of an eagle’s head pointing towards the same direction.

However, when comparing signs in conflict in terms of their figurative elements, the Office considers the latter as images: if they match in one, separately recognisable, element or have the same or a similar contour, it is likely that some visual similarity will be found. Contrary to the opponent’s view, the fact that two signs depict the same object or animal, as in the present case, does not automatically lead to a finding of similarity between them.

The signs' figurative elements display striking differences. The earlier mark is characterised by the use of thick golden strokes reminiscent of paintbrush marks. Its figurative device resembles a silhouette, with the details of the eagle's head, including its eyes and nostrils, entirely omitted. Conversely, although highly stylised, the contested sign's figurative device presents a more realistic representation of the same animal, depicted through the use of thick, black, wavy lines. As a result, these figurative devices barely lead to a visual similarity between the signs, as they do not match in any separately recognisable element and hardly can be considered to have a similar contour.

The signs’ remaining elements and aspects do not bring them closer together. The verbal elements ‘EL ÁGUILA’ and ‘ATHLETIC CLUB PALERMO’ do not share any letter in the same position and do not resemble each other. Finally, the signs employ different colours, backgrounds and typefaces, which further contribute to a radically different overall impression.

From this perspective, the case law invoked by the opponent, according to which two marks should be considered similar anytime they are at least partially identical as regards one or more relevant aspects (02/11/2003, T-286/02, Kiap Mou, EU:T:2003:311, § 38 and the case-law cited; 15/02/2007, T-501/04, Royal, EU:T:2007:54, § 44 and the case-law cited; and 06/05/2008, T-246/06, Reverie, EU:T:2008:141, § 61 and the caselaw cited; and 14/04/2011, T-466/08, Acno focus, EU:T:2011:182, § 52 and the case law cited therein), is irrelevant for the purpose of the present comparison, as the signs share no identical element.

Therefore, if not entirely dissimilar, the signs can only be considered visually similar to a faint degree.

Aurally, the signs’ pronunciation differs in the sound of all their letters, namely /EL ÁGUILA/ and /ATHLETIC CLUB PALERMO/. The fact that the signs have some letters in common in different positions does not lead to any similarity between them, considering that the alphabet is made up of a limited number of letters and consumers will not perceive the presence of the same letters in different positions as an indication of similarity. Finally, it should also be noted that the signs have different lengths and numbers of syllables, which leads to a clear difference in rhythm.

Furthermore, the opponent’s claim that ‘(…) it is very likely that relevant consumers will refer to the contested brand as the one with the eagle’ is untenable. According to the Office’s practice, figurative elements are not subject to a phonetic assessment, as established in the judgements of 07/02/2012, T-424/10, Éléphants dans un rectangle, EU:T:2012:58, § 46; 08/10/2014, T-342/12, Star, EU:T:2014:858, § 48; 30/09/2015, T-364/13, KAJMAN / Device of a crocodile et al., EU:T:2015:738, § 46; 25/11/2015, T-320/14, Device of two wavy black lines (fig.) / Device of wavy black link (fig.), EU:T:2015:882, § 45-46.

Therefore, the signs are aurally dissimilar.

Conceptually, reference is made to the previous assertions concerning the semantic content conveyed by the marks. The signs are conceptually similar to at least an average degree, since they will both associated with ‘an eagle’ and the additional meanings conveyed by the contested sign will not offset the perception of this shared concept.

As the signs have been found similar in at least one aspect of the comparison, the examination of likelihood of confusion will proceed.

d) Distinctiveness of the earlier mark

The distinctiveness of the earlier mark is one of the factors to be taken into account in the global assessment of likelihood of confusion.

According to the opponent, the earlier trade mark has a reputation in Spain in connection with all the goods for which it is registered, namely beers. This claim must be properly considered given that the distinctiveness of the earlier trade mark must be taken into account in the assessment of likelihood of confusion. Indeed, the more distinctive the earlier mark, the greater will be the likelihood of confusion, and therefore marks with a highly distinctive character because of the recognition they possess on the market, enjoy broader protection than marks with a less distinctive character (29/09/1998, C‑39/97, Canon, EU:C:1998:442, § 18).

The enhanced distinctiveness / reputation of the earlier trade mark should exist at the time of filing of the contested EUTM application (or any priority date). In principle, it is sufficient that the opponent show that its mark had acquired enhanced distinctiveness on that date. Enhanced distinctiveness should also exist at the time when the opposition decision is taken. However, in principle, this will be assumed unless the applicant claims and proves any subsequent loss of enhanced distinctiveness.

In the present case, the contested trade mark was filed on 27/09/2023. Therefore, the opponent was required to prove that the trade mark on which the opposition is based had a reputation or at least enjoyed a high degree of recognition among the relevant public prior to that date.

The evidence must also show that the reputation or the high degree of recognition among the relevant public was acquired for the goods to which the opponent’s claim relates and that have been found similar to the contested goods, namely:

Class 32: Beers.

As a preliminary remark, the Opposition Division acknowledges that a significant part of the evidence submitted is in Spanish and that the opponent has not provided a translation into the language of the proceedings. However, since the untranslated evidence does not materially affect the outcome of the present opposition and the applicant has not requested a translation, the Opposition Division will take into account for the purpose of the present proceedings without requesting a translation and will describe it in English. This solution obeys reasons of procedural economy by avoiding the reopening of the proceedings without affecting the applicant’s right to be heard.

The opponent submitted the following evidence:

	Its observations of 03/03/2026, where it summarises and explains the evidence submitted and provides an overview of the history and success of the earlier mark. In particular, the document recounts the earlier mark’s achievements in the period between 1907 and 1990.

	Annex 2: It contains the following documents:

o	A slide dated December 2009, showing a picture of the brewery El Águila, located in Madrid, as it appeared at the beginning of the 20th century. The building is now the headquarters of the Joaquín Regional Library.

o	A slide dated July 2006, showing a picture of the façade of an ancient brewery called Fábrica de Delicias. The picture is undated.

o	Spanish Wikipedia page of ‘Cerveza El Águila’. The first sentence of the page stipulates that ‘Cerveza El Águila is brand of Spanish beer that was founded in Madrid in 1900 and relaunched in 2019’.

o	A slide of unidentified origin, which defines El Águila as one of the main beer brands in Spain and containing a map of El Águila breweries in the Spanish territory. However, the pictures of the breweries on the map refer to the period between 1912 and 1962.

o	A printout from an unidentified website. The document stipulates that ‘the consolidated net profit of the El Águila brewing group amounted to 2 865 million pesetas between January and September of the current year. This represents a 95% increase compared to the figures achieved in the first nine months of 1998 [emphasis added]’.

	Annex 3: A ‘Certificate of brand recognition and reputation’ issued by the Chamber of Commerce, Industry, Services and Navigation of Seville on 22/02/2021. The certificate stipulates that based on the evidence provided by the certificate applicant, the mark ‘ÁGUILA’ is ‘widely known and reputed in the beverage sector, especially beers in the territorial demarcation of Seville’. The evidence on which the decision is based is not enclosed.

	Annex 4: Several Opposition decisions of the Spanish Patent and Trade Mark Office, listed below. The opposed marks were denied registration because of the existence of a likelihood of confusion with the opponent’s mark ‘EL AGUILA’ and because they unfairly profited from the reputation of that mark. The evidence on which the decisions were based are neither enclosed nor described in the text of the decisions.

o	15/03/2022, 430520/5, ‘PINO DE LAS ÁGUILAS’ (word mark);

o	14/01/2021, 414568/2 ‘AGILA’ (word mark);

o	17/12/2019, 4011396/5, ‘PICO L'AGUILA’ (word mark);

o	14/12/2016, 367586/6, ‘AGUILA SUSHI’ (word mark);

o	28/09/2016, 956987, ‘GOLDEN EAGLE.’ (figurative mark);

o	10/06/2013, 3058122, ‘CERVEZA ASTURIANA EL AGUILA DEL COLLOTO’ (figurative mark);

o	31/10/2005, 2624670, ‘CERVEZA-AGUILA CERVECERIA DE BARRANQUILA’ (figurative mark).

	Annex 5: Witness statement of 15/02/2021, signed by the general director of DENTSU MEDIA S.L. The deponent declares that the opponent has invested around 1 850 00 euros to advertise the mark ‘El Águila’ between 2019 and 2021.

	Annex 6: A selection of documents:

o	A slide with advertisements of the earlier mark.

o	Printouts from the X account of ‘Cerveza el Aguila’, extracted on 10/09/2025. The document shows that the page was followed by only 677 users on that date.

o	Undated printouts from the Facebook account of ‘Cerveza el Águila’. The document shows that the page was followed by 8 196 users.

o	Undated printouts from the Instagram account of ‘Cerveza el Águila’, extracted on 10/09/2025. The document shows that the page was followed by over 22 000 users.

o	Printouts of a Google search performed by using the word query ‘el aguila’. The search returned over 31 000 000 results.

	Annex 7: Thumbnails of video advertisements of the beer ‘el Águila’, uploaded on YouTube. The number of views is rather low, between 290 and 2 500.

	Annex 8: A selection of articles, which include both independent articles and pieces that have been sponsored by the opponent.

o	Victor M. Osorio, ‘El Águila beer reaches over 500 000 households’ (28/11/2020, Expansión), stipulating that ‘Heineken has exceeded the targets it had set itself less than two years after the launch of El Águila beer’.

o	Jaime de las Heras, ‘A new flight for beer El Águila’ (17/03/2019, lainformacion.com), stipulating that the beer was ‘a well-known and recognisable brand throughout the state’ and ‘a crowd favourite’. The article recognizes that the production of the beer was interrupted at the beginning of the 21st century and that restarted in 2019, with a new logo.

o	Tomás Monago, ‘El Alcázar and El Águila beers are now on the market’ (16/03/2019, Diario de Sevilla). The article indicates that ‘El Águila’ beer held a 30% share of the Spanish market in the 1960s, it was acquired by Heineken in 1984 and that its production was phased out from 2000, to be eventually withdrawn from the market to be replaced with the beer ‘Amstel’. However, the decision to reintroduce it in the market was due the consumer’s affection towards this brand.

	Annex 9: Printouts of the webpages of retailers such as Carrefour, Mercadona and El Campo, containing offers for sale of various formats and kinds of ‘El Águila’ beers.

	Annex 10: Awards and evaluations:

o	An evaluation of the beers ‘El Águila 1900’ and ‘El Águila Sin Filtrar’, carried out in the context of the ‘European Beer Star 2020’.

o	‘Gold Quality Award – 59th World Selection of Beers, Waters and Soft Drinks 2020’.

o	Bronze award, for the beers ‘El Águila Lager’ and ‘El Águila Sin Filtrar’.

o	‘Superior taste award’ (2020) for ‘El Águila 1900’ and ‘El Águila Sin Filtrar’.

o	‘World Beer Awards Spain – Silver for ‘El Águila Sin Filtrar’.

	Annex 11: An article titled ‘Heineken signs on as the first sponsor of the new Roig Arena’ dated 29/01/2025, mentioning that ‘Heineken will be the exclusive beer supplier for all of its cultural and sporting events, along with its Heineken, Amstel, and El Águila brands’.

Having examined the material listed above, the Opposition Division concludes that the evidence submitted by the opponent does not demonstrate that the earlier trade mark acquired a high degree of distinctiveness through its use.

As a starting point, the evidence submitted shows that use of the earlier trade mark was discontinued at the beginning of the 2000s and resumed only in 2019. This places a significant evidential burden on the opponent, which must demonstrate either that the earlier mark acquired market recognition in less than four years or that the recognition it had previously enjoyed survived a twenty-year absence from the market.

The evidence submitted falls short of discharging that burden.

The documents in Annex 2 relate to the history of the beer ‘El Águila’ by presenting pictures of the past locations of its breweries and referring to the commercial volume achieved by the brand up to 1999. However, they contain no meaningful information or data that alludes to the success or recognition of the brand after that date. 

This narrative is supported by the articles and advertisements contained in Annex 8. Most of these articles refer to the earlier fame and success of the mark but do not provide compelling evidence of its current reputation or commercial success.

In this regard, the few articles referring to the volume of sales achieved under the mark following its relaunch in 2019 do not demonstrate a particularly high level of commercial success. In particular, the fact that El Águila beers reached more than 500 000 households in 2020 does not establish that the opponent had secured a consolidated position in the relevant market. It is common knowledge that Spain has a population of over 40 million inhabitants and that the Spanish beer market is substantial in size and characterised by intense competition among numerous undertakings. Against this background, a mere reference to the number of households reached, without any supporting information regarding the actual sales volume and/or market share achieved, constitutes an overly generic indicator that cannot support a finding of enhanced distinctiveness.

Admittedly, the documents submitted suggest that the earlier mark was advertised in well-known magazines and media outlets, such as Elle, Men's Health and Vogue. This demonstrates that a certain level of promotional effort was made in relation to the mark. However, the opponent has not provided any information concerning the actual reach or circulation of the publications and advertisements submitted. Consequently, the Opposition Division is unable to determine whether the advertising material was in fact seen by a significant proportion of the relevant Spanish public.

Furthermore, the documents were published in 2020, indicating that consumers had been exposed to the opponent's advertising campaign for only a relatively limited period of time. Finally, a significant proportion of the documents merely announces the return of the opponent's brand, thereby confirming that the opponent's products had only recently re-entered the market when the advertisements were published.

The same considerations diminish the probative value of the witness statement contained in Annex 5. According to that statement, the mark was advertised for a period of only three years. Moreover, given that the beginning of that period coincides with the relaunch of the opponent's brand, it is likely that the advertising campaign was primarily intended to inform consumers of the return of ‘El Águila’. This interpretation is consistent with the content of the advertising material submitted in Annex 8.

As regards Annexes 6 and 7, the printouts from social media, search engines and content-sharing platforms do not demonstrate that the opponent's brand has achieved a significant level of success online. For example, the number of followers of the opponent's social media accounts is not particularly high, especially when considered in the context of the large number of consumers potentially interested in this particular beverage sector.

In any event, although websites and social media may constitute an independent source of evidence in respect of information generated by the platforms themselves, which cannot be controlled or altered by the owner of a page or account (24/10/2017, T-202/16, coffee inn (fig.) / coffee in (fig.) et al., EU:T:2017:750, § 51), it is only where the opponent has submitted website or social media analytics reports that such evidence may reliably demonstrate the extent to which the relevant pages have been visited and the characteristics of those visits (19/10/2022, T-275/21, DEVICE OF A CHEQUERBOARD PATTERN (fig.), EU:T:2022:654, §§ 80, 82).

In the absence of such analytics, the Opposition Division cannot draw any conclusions regarding matters such as the number of page views, visits, the duration of those visits, or the geographical location of the users. This significantly reduces the probative value of the evidence submitted.

Annexes 3 and 4 show that Spanish authorities - specifically the Seville Chamber of Commerce and the Spanish IP Office – consider that the mark ‘El Águila’ enjoys reputation in Spain.

It is reminded that that decisions of national courts and national offices regarding conflicts between identical or similar trade marks at national level do not have a binding effect on the Office since the European Union trade mark regime is an autonomous system, which applies independently of any national system (13/09/2010, T‑292/08, OFTEN / OLTEN et al., EU:T:2010:399). Even though previous national decisions are not binding, their reasoning and outcome should be duly considered, particularly when the decision has been taken in the Member State that is relevant to the proceedings.

There might be differences between the substantive and procedural conditions applicable in national proceedings and those applied in opposition proceedings before the Office. Firstly, there may be differences as to how the requirement of reputation is defined or interpreted. Secondly, the weight the Office gives to the evidence is not necessarily the same as the weight given to it in national proceedings. Furthermore, national instances may be able to take into account ex officio facts known to them directly, whereas, under Article 95 EUTMR, the Office may not. Consequently, the probative value of national decisions should be assessed on the basis of their contents, including the specific evidence submitted by the parties, and may vary depending on the case.

The documents submitted do not explain the legal criteria adopted by the Spanish authorities in establishing reputation and do not refer or describe the evidence submitted in those proceedings. As a result, the Opposition Division cannot verify whether those decisions comply with the criteria and legal standards adopted by Office. This greatly reduces the relevance and probatory value of those decisions.

Annex 9 merely shows that the opponent's products were available for purchase online. However, it provides no information as to the reputation of the earlier mark or the commercial success achieved under it.

Annex 10 contains awards and certifications attesting to the quality of the opponent's beers. However, the fact that those products have received recognition for their quality does not automatically establish that the earlier mark is known to the relevant public. Rather, it merely demonstrates that the opponent's goods satisfy certain quality or technical standards.

Annex 11 falls outside the relevant period. Moreover, it mainly concerns the involvement of ‘Heineken’ and refers to events that had not yet taken place at the time of publication. Accordingly, its probative value is very limited, if not altogether irrelevant for the purposes of the present proceedings.

To summarise, the opponent’s claims that ‘the popularity of the opposing trade mark is beyond doubt or discussion, since we are faced with one of the most prestigious, distinctive signs in the national and international market of the alcoholic beverages sector [emphasis added]’ is at odds with the narrative described by the opponent’s evidence. Such an exceptional degree of recognition should be capable of being demonstrated by evidence establishing the mark's actual and current recognition among the relevant public, rather than by materials referring to its former success or merely promoting the relaunch of the opponent's brand.

In this regard, any claim that the earlier mark enjoys an enhanced degree of distinctiveness or a reputation must be substantiated by solid and objective evidence. The Opposition Division cannot simply presume that a mark relaunched in 2019, following an absence from the market of approximately 20 years, had regained a significant level of market recognition by the relevant date solely on account of its historical reputation. In the present case, the evidence submitted does not establish that the earlier mark had secured a dominant or consolidated position in the market at the relevant date or that it was known to a significant part of the relevant public.

Consequently, the assessment of the earlier mark's distinctiveness must be based on its inherent distinctiveness. For the reasons set out in section (c) above, the earlier mark must be regarded as possessing a normal degree of distinctiveness in relation to the relevant goods, namely beers.

e) Global assessment, other arguments and conclusion

The goods in Class 32 are similar and they target the public at large, whose degree of attention is average. The rest of the contested services in Class 41 are dissimilar to the opponent’s goods. The signs are visually similar to a faint degree (if not entirely dissimilar) and phonetically dissimilar. However, they are conceptually similar to at least an average degree. The earlier mark has a normal degree of inherent distinctiveness.

A conceptual similarity between signs with analogous semantic content may give rise to a likelihood of confusion only where the earlier mark is particularly distinctive (11/11/1997, C‑251/95, Sabèl, EU:C:1997:528, § 24). Conversely, in the absence of a particularly high degree of distinctiveness, the fact that the signs share the same distinctive concept does not lead to a likelihood of confusion unless the shared concept is accompanied by visual similarities between the signs.

As already explained in section c) of the present decision, the conceptual similarities between the signs are not backed up by a sufficient degree of similarity at the visual and phonetical level. The striking differences between the signs will allow consumers to safely differentiate when finalising the relevant purchases. The fact that average consumers rarely have the chance to make a direct comparison between different marks but must trust in their imperfect recollection of them (22/06/1999, C‑342/97, Lloyd Schuhfabrik, EU:C:1999:323, § 26) does not put this finding into question, since the differences between the signs are memorable and will be easily retained by consumers, even in their imperfect recollection.

In the same vein, it would be unreasonable to conceive that the relevant consumer will perceive the contested mark as a sub-brand, a variation of the earlier mark, configured in a different way according to the type of goods or services that it designates (23/10/2002, T‑104/01, Miss Fifties (fig.) / Fifties, EU:T:2002:262, § 49). The signs are too far apart for consumers to believe that they originate from the same or economically linked undertakings, as it cannot be considered a standard market practice for undertakings to alter their marks to such an extent that they would only coincide in the presence of a completely different stylisation of the same animal.

For the sake of completeness, even if the Opposition Division's assessment regarding the enhanced distinctiveness of the earlier mark were considered to be erroneous, this would not affect the outcome of the present decision. An enhanced degree of distinctiveness increases the likelihood that the relevant public will recall the earlier mark, recognise its characteristics and establish an association with similar signs. However, enhanced distinctiveness does not diminish the significance of the differences between the signs. This is particularly true in the present case, where those differences are striking and clearly outweigh the limited similarities identified between the signs.

The opponent refers to previous decisions of the Office of and of national authorities to support its arguments regarding the similarity between the signs and the existence of a likelihood of confusion.

Decisions of national courts and national offices regarding conflicts between identical or similar trade marks at national level do not have a binding effect on the Office since the European Union trade mark regime is an autonomous system, which applies independently of any national system (13/09/2010, T‑292/08, OFTEN / OLTEN et al., EU:T:2010:399). Similarly, the Office is not bound by its previous decisions, as each case has to be dealt with separately and with regard to its particularities (30/06/2004, T-281/02, Mehr für Ihr Geld, EU:T:2004:198).

Even though previous decisions are not binding, their reasoning and outcome should be duly considered. 

In the present case, the previous cases referred to by the opponent are not relevant to the present proceedings, as they all concern cases where the signs shared or overlap in their verbal elements. This is not the case here, given the complete and outstanding differences between the signs’ verbal elements ‘EL ÁGUILA’ and ‘ATHLETIC CLUB PALERMO’.

Considering all the above, there is no likelihood of confusion on the part of the public. Therefore, the opposition must be rejected.

The opponent has also based its opposition on the earlier Spanish trade mark registration ‘EL AGUILA’ (word mark), registered for the following services:

Class 41: Publication, editing of reports and writing of texts; education, entertainment and sports activity services; ticket booking services for educational, entertainment and sports activities and events; translation and interpretation; education, entertainment and sports activities; creation [writing] portable audio files [podcasts]; providing publications from a global computer network or online that can be consulted; facilitation of electronic publications; publication of catalogs; publication of posters; publication of technical sheets; organization of conferences, exhibitions and competitions; amusement and theme parks, fairs, zoos and museums; live performance services; leasing services related to e equipment facilities for education, entertainment, sports and culture; gaming or betting services; video game services; sports services and physical maintenance; celebration of competitions online; organization of talks and conferences; organization of leisure competitions; organization of competitions [educational or recreational activities]; wine tastings [educational services]; organization and conduct of wine tastings for entertainment purposes; publication of newspapers, periodic publications, catalogs and brochures; beer tastings; water tastings; tastings; food and drink tastings; leisure, education and instruction services; audio, video and photography production; publication services for digital entertainment, audio and video content.

This mark cover goods that are identical or similar to the contested services in Class 41.

However, it is even less similar to less similar to the contested mark. This is because it merely consists of a verbal element which, as already explained in section c) of the present decision, does not share any considerable point of contact with the contested sign’s verbal element ‘ATHLETIC CLUB PALERMO’. As a result, these marks are visually and aurally dissimilar. Although they both convey the meaning of an eagle, this coincidence is insufficient to lead to a likelihood of confusion, for the reasons already discussed in the present decision.

REPUTATION — ARTICLE 8(5) EUTMR 

In relation to Article 8(5) EUTMR, the opponent invoked earlier Spanish trade mark registration No 4 023 520  (figurative mark).

According to Article 8(5) EUTMR, upon opposition by the proprietor of a registered earlier trade mark within the meaning of Article 8(2) EUTMR, the contested trade mark will not be registered where it is identical with, or similar to, an earlier trade mark, irrespective of whether the goods or services for which it is applied are identical with, similar to or not similar to those for which the earlier trade mark is registered, where, in the case of an earlier European Union trade mark, the trade mark has a reputation in the Union or, in the case of an earlier national trade mark, the trade mark has a reputation in the Member State concerned and where the use without due cause of the contested trade mark would take unfair advantage of, or be detrimental to, the distinctive character or the repute of the earlier trade mark.

Therefore, the grounds for refusal of Article 8(5) EUTMR are only applicable when the following conditions are met.

	The signs must be either identical or similar. 

	The opponent’s trade mark must have a reputation. The reputation must also be prior to the filing of the contested trade mark; it must exist in the territory concerned and for the goods and/or services on which the opposition is based. 

	Risk of injury: use of the contested trade mark would take unfair advantage of, or be detrimental to, the distinctive character or repute of the earlier trade mark.

The abovementioned requirements are cumulative and, therefore, the absence of any one of them will lead to the rejection of the opposition under Article 8(5) EUTMR (16/12/2010, T-357/08, BOTOCYL / BOTOX, EU:T:2010:529, § 41; 16/12/2010, T-345/08, BOTOLIST / BOTOX, EU:T:2010:529, § 41). However, the fulfilment of all the abovementioned conditions may not be sufficient. The opposition may still fail if the applicant establishes due cause for the use of the contested trade mark.

In the present case, the applicant did not claim to have due cause for using the contested mark. Therefore, in the absence of any indications to the contrary, it must be assumed that no due cause exists.

f) Reputation of the earlier trade mark

The evidence submitted by the opponent to prove the reputation and highly distinctive character of the earlier trade mark has already been examined above under the grounds of Article 8(1)(b) EUTMR. Reference is made to those findings, which are equally valid for Article 8(5) EUTMR, also considering that the assessment of reputation involves a higher threshold than enhanced distinctiveness.

Therefore, the Opposition Division finds that the evidence submitted by the opponent does not demonstrate that the earlier trade mark acquired a reputation.

g) Conclusion as to Article 8(5) EUTMR

As seen above, it is a requirement for the opposition to be successful under Article 8(5) EUTMR that the earlier trade mark has a reputation. Since it has not been established that the earlier trade mark has a reputation, one of the necessary conditions contained in Article 8(5) EUTMR is not fulfilled, and the opposition must be rejected.

COSTS

According to Article 109(1) EUTMR, the losing party in opposition proceedings must bear the fees and costs incurred by the other party.

Since the opponent is the losing party, it must bear the costs incurred by the applicant in the course of these proceedings.

According to Article 109(7) EUTMR and Article 18(1)(c)(i) EUTMIR, the costs to be paid to the applicant are the costs of representation, which are to be fixed on the basis of the maximum rate set therein.
